newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu says no quick fix for Israel-PLO crisis.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says no quick fix for Israel-PLO crisis.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday it would "take some time" before a U.S. envoy would get Israel and the PLO to talk peace again.

The Israeli leader also said he was proud of his March decision that sent bulldozers to carve out a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, plunging peacemaking between the sides into deep crisis.
"I'm proud that I approved the building in Jerusalem which clarified to the entire world our commitment to the unity of the city," Netanyahu told Israel Radio.
He dismissed the idea the settlement stopped peacemaking.
"No process was stopped. If that stopped the process, there is no process," Netanyahu said.
He said difficulties had arisen because final status matters like the fate of Jerusalem and the nature of the permanent Palestinian political entity were next up for negotiation.
Netanyahu says Jerusalem can never be divided and he opposes the Palestinian goal of a sovereign state.

Palestinians want East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state in the West Bank and Gaza Strip. Israel captured the Gaza Strip and the West Bank including Arab East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war.
PLO and Western officials said envoy Dennis Ross was trying to arrange a meeting of Israelis and Palestinians to discuss the issues that led to the two-month-old freeze in negotiations.
Talks are also stuck over Israel's demand for a Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) crackdown on "terrorism".
Asked if Ross' second mission in a month was making progress, Netanyahu said: "Well, I think that this is going to take some time. It's not happening overnight."
Negotiations have been largely stalled since the start of the Jewish settlement and an attack on a Tel Aviv cafe later in March that killed a Palestinian bomber and three Israelis.
Ross was to meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in the West Bank city of Ramallah later on Sunday.
"Ross presented some ideas on how to restart contacts with Israel," a PLO official, who declined to be identified, said.
"He suggested a meeting, not negotiations, between PLO and Israeli negotiators attended by Ross himself to probe into the issues that led to the crisis in the peace talks."
Western officials said Ross was awaiting a response from Arafat on whether Palestinians would meet the Israelis.

Officials said the PLO was willing to meet the Israelis on condition the talks tackled the issues of Jewish settlements in Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and the Gaza Strip and only after receiving U.S. guarantees the meeting would lead to a halt in settlement activities.
But Israel said the meeting would have a different agenda -- not including Jewish settlement of occupied land.
Israeli government spokesman Moshe Fogel said his side would raise "fighting terror and Palestinian violations to the agreement". Fogel said there would be no halt to settlement.
Palestinians see Jewish settlement in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank including Jerusalem as pre-empting the outcome of final peace negotiations that have yet to take place.
Netanyahu, asked by Israel's army radio if he would ever evacuate Jewish settlers from occupied Arab lands, said:
"We said we would weigh in the government establishment of new settlements but we did not say we would consider evacuation...I have no intention to evacuate any settlement."
Since 1967, more than 130,000 Israelis have settled amidst nearly two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
